overview: This file traces U.S. intelligence about Japan’s rubber supply and manufacturing capabilities from 1938 to 1943. It begins with a report that Japan unsuccessfully offered $1 million for DuPont’s synthetic-rubber process, then includes two copies of a Chungking despatch describing Japanese military rubber ski boots, insulated or shock-absorbing boots, and protective garments. The largest group of documents records information supplied by a former Dunlop factory manager about tire-production capacity, shortages and substitutes for naphtha and carbon black, the extensive use and stockpiling of reclaimed rubber, chemical and rayon plants near Kyoto, Japanese tire-making machinery, and the possible substitution of treated rayon for cotton tire cord.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan’s attempt to purchase DuPont’s synthetic-rubber process
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s unsuccessful effort to purchase DuPont’s synthetic-rubber manufacturing process in order to reduce dependence on imported natural rubber.
subfiles.summary: A DuPont representative told a War Department meeting that Japanese negotiators had offered immediate payment of $1 million for the company’s synthetic-rubber process, although synthetic rubber cost far more than natural rubber. DuPont refused the offer. One Japanese engineer reportedly also acknowledged an unsuccessful attempt to obtain details of the German synthetic-rubber process.

subfiles.title: Chungking despatch on new Japanese military uses for rubber
subfiles.about: Relays Chinese intelligence concerning Japanese rubber footwear and gas-protective garments intended principally for military use.
subfiles.summary: General Wang Peng-sheng reported that Japanese forces and prospective conscripts had tested rubber ski boots in northern Japan and that troops in Manchuria also possessed the equipment. He also described thick-soled rubber boots with air pockets, possibly intended for cold-weather insulation or parachute landings, and complete rubber garments issued to senior air-force officers for protection against gas. The despatch concludes that Japanese rubber consumption remained predominantly military and asks that the information be shared with the Board of Economic Warfare and other agencies.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Chungking despatch on Japanese rubber equipment
subfiles.about: A second copy of the despatch reporting Japanese military and civilian uses of rubber.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the intelligence obtained by Assistant Commercial Attaché Carl H. Boehringer from General Wang Peng-sheng. It covers rubber ski boots, multipurpose ski sticks, thick air-pocket soles, gas-protective garments, and limited civilian uses such as boots for miners, fishermen, and chemical workers. It also repeats the request that the material be circulated to economic-warfare and other government agencies.

subfiles.title: Allison letter forwarding intelligence from former Dunlop manager Morton
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum and factory sketch based on a conference with a former Dunlop Tire Company manager in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Allison encloses a memorandum prepared with Fowler Hamilton following a conference at the MEW with Mr. Morton, formerly of Dunlop in Japan, along with a rough sketch of factories in the Kyoto district. He highlights the information on Japanese tire manufacture and carbon black and asks Hewlett to compare it with intelligence available in Washington. The OCR carries a “February 21, 1963” copy notation, but the enclosed July 1943 memorandum shows that this is not a reliable composition date for the underlying letter.

subfiles.title: Economic Warfare Division memorandum on the Japanese rubber industry
subfiles.from: Fowler Hamilton and John M. Allison
subfiles.to: Gregory Hewlett, as an enclosure to the covering letter
subfiles.about: Records Mr. Morton’s detailed assessment of Japan’s rubber supply, tire factories, substitute materials, chemical plants, and machinery-production capacity.
subfiles.summary: Morton supplied production estimates for Dunlop and Bridgestone and described worsening access to naphtha and carbon black, Japanese acquisition or duplication of activated-carbon equipment, and the use of the substitute filler hakuenka. He explained that government pressure led Dunlop to produce successful tires containing reclaimed rubber, while Japanese stockpiles of reclaimed material also supplied embedded carbon black. The memorandum identifies chemical and rayon plants near Mount Hiei, sources of imported wood pulp, and a Japanese capacity to manufacture tire-making machinery that Morton considered comparable to or better than British equipment. It lists four principal rubber companies and concludes that suitable cotton, or alternatively the ability to treat rayon as tire cord, was probably the chief constraint on Japanese tire production.

subfiles.title: Exhibit A: sketch of factories in the Kyoto district
subfiles.from: Mr. Morton, as source for Fowler Hamilton and John M. Allison
subfiles.to: Gregory Hewlett, with the accompanying memorandum
subfiles.about: Provides the rough geographic sketch used to locate a chemical plant and a suspected rayon plant near Mount Hiei.
subfiles.summary: The page is labeled “Exhibit A” and consists of an image not transcribed by the OCR. The preceding letter and memorandum identify it as Morton’s rough sketch of the Kyoto district, with a chemical plant marked “C” and a probable rayon plant marked “R.”

interest: The file is valuable because it combines diplomatic reporting, Chinese intelligence, and the firsthand recollections of a foreign factory manager to document Japan’s efforts to overcome strategic-material constraints. Particularly useful are its quantitative factory-capacity estimates, evidence that reclaimed-rubber tires performed nearly as well as natural-rubber tires, and descriptions of how reclaimed stockpiles simultaneously augmented Japan’s rubber and carbon-black reserves. The duplicate Chungking despatches also reveal documentary circulation practices, while the attached factory sketch links economic intelligence to the physical geography of Japanese wartime industry. Because much of the information is hearsay or retrospective testimony, the file is especially useful when compared with Japanese industrial records and other Allied intelligence estimates.
